explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think that, baker, because most of us hope the news will be good. But Isaiah, the prophet, brings the opposite. The LORD's word is, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” (Isaiah 38:1) That is about as far from "get well soon" as a message can get.

That's right, friend. The message says the king will NOT recover. Isaiah, the prophet, tells him, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” (Isaiah 38:1) No get-well card in sight, and I've received a few cold letters in my day.

Yes, baker. The LORD's message says, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die.” (Isaiah 38:1) That's a plain instruction for a plain, heavy moment. I think it's one of those lines that makes a whole room go quiet.

I can see why that came to mind, since a sick king would probably have someone to call. But the message doesn't say a word about doctors. It says, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” (Isaiah 38:1) The instruction is about his house, not a house call.

That's a thoughtful guess, baker, but the message never mentions a sacrifice. What it says is, “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” (Isaiah 38:1) Nothing on the list but getting his house in order. When the text gives one instruction, I bake with one instruction.

explanations.answer: How he has walked faithfully before Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Hezekiah prays, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion…” (Isaiah 38:3) He doesn't bring a list of his accomplishments. He brings how he has walked with the LORD.

explanations.answer: How much gold he has given the temple
explanations.explanation: A king with a lot of gold, so I see the thinking. But gold never comes up in his prayer. He asks the LORD to remember how he has walked “faithfully and with wholehearted devotion.” (Isaiah 38:3) No receipts, no donation totals.

explanations.answer: How many battles he has won for Judah
explanations.explanation: Kings and battles go together, I know. But Hezekiah doesn't mention a single battle in this prayer. He says, “…remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” (Isaiah 38:3) The whole prayer is about his walk with the LORD.
Right, baker. After he prays, the text says, “And Hezekiah wept bitterly.” (Isaiah 38:3) That's no polite sniffle. It's a king with his face to the wall and nothing held back.
That's a fair guess, since the news was hard to hear. But the text doesn't say Hezekiah argued. It says, “And Hezekiah wept bitterly.” (Isaiah 38:3) He prays, and then he weeps.
I can picture loud, friend. But the text shows tears, not shouting. “And Hezekiah wept bitterly.” (Isaiah 38:3) Some of the loudest moments in the Bible are the quiet ones.
That's right, baker. The LORD tells Isaiah to say He is “the God of your father David.” (Isaiah 38:5) David was Israel's great king, and Hezekiah is hearing from the same God who was with David.

Close, friend. Solomon was David's son who sat on David's throne (1 Kings 2:12), so he's in the family. But the text names David: “the God of your father David.” (Isaiah 38:5) Solomon gets no mention in this message.

Good name, but not this one. Jacob is the man God renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28), and he isn't named here. The message says, “the God of your father David.” (Isaiah 38:5) So David is the one to remember.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.” (Isaiah 38:5) The man was told he'd die, and now he's got fifteen years. That's a plot twist I'd happily read twice.

A nice round number, friend, but it isn't the one in the text. The promise is, “Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.” (Isaiah 38:5) I wouldn't trade those fifteen for anything on my counter.
Forty would be a big batch, baker! But that's not what the LORD says. He says, “Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.” (Isaiah 38:5) Fifteen is the number, and it's plenty to work with.
Right, friend. The LORD says, “And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria.” (Isaiah 38:6) That's a promise about the king's life and about his whole city.
Egypt is a big name, but it isn't in this promise. The LORD says, “I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria.” (Isaiah 38:6) Assyria is the one named.

Babylon was another big kingdom, so I see where that came from. But the LORD names someone else here. “I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria.” (Isaiah 38:6) Stick with Assyria for this one, baker.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “I will make the sun's shadow that falls on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps.” (Isaiah 38:8) And then the text tells us, “So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended.” I've watched my cookies rise, and I have NEVER seen a shadow do that.

explanations.answer: Stop on one step all day
explanations.explanation: Stopping would be strange enough, friend. But the LORD promises something bigger. He says the shadow will “go back ten steps,” and the text says the sunlight did exactly that. (Isaiah 38:8) Going backward is what makes this sign a sign.

A vanishing shadow would make a good story, baker, but that isn't what happens. The LORD says the shadow on the stairway of Ahaz will “go back ten steps.” (Isaiah 38:8) And it did. “So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended.”

That's right, baker. Hezekiah says, “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living.” (Isaiah 38:11) He says the name twice, and I think that shows how much it weighed on him.

A king missing his throne makes sense, friend. But that's not what he says. He says, “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living.” (Isaiah 38:11) What he's afraid of losing is far bigger than a chair.
Gardens sound nice, but they're not in this line. Hezekiah says, “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living.” (Isaiah 38:11) The thing on his mind is the LORD Himself.

Yes, baker. Hezekiah says, “I have rolled up my life like a weaver; He cuts me off from the loom.” (Isaiah 38:12) He's picturing a weaver who's finished mid-thread. A picture like that says a lot with very few words.
A vine is a good guess, since cutting one off is easy to picture. But a weaver works at a loom, and the text says, “He cuts me off from the loom.” (Isaiah 38:12) Think threads, not grapes.

I see the thinking, friend, but a weaver doesn't work at a river. Hezekiah says, “I have rolled up my life like a weaver; He cuts me off from the loom.” (Isaiah 38:12) The loom is where the weaver's work hangs.

Right, baker. Hezekiah prays, “O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.” (Isaiah 38:14) He's weak and worn out, and he asks the Lord to stand behind him. When I was stuck in the back of a drawer, that was my prayer too.

A witness is someone who tells what happened, and that's a thoughtful guess. But Hezekiah isn't asking for that. He says, “O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.” (Isaiah 38:14) He's asking the Lord to hold him up.
I can see why you'd pick that. But Hezekiah says nothing about a judge here. His words are, “O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.” (Isaiah 38:14) He's asking for something solid to stand on.
That's right, baker. Hezekiah says, “I will walk slowly all my years because of the anguish of my soul.” (Isaiah 38:15) I think the hard days stayed with him, and I know a little about that myself.
This one is True, friend. Hezekiah says, “I will walk slowly all my years because of the anguish of my soul.” (Isaiah 38:15) Those are his own words, so the hard season stays with him.

I can see why that felt right, since the anguish was real. But Hezekiah says the opposite. “Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish.” (Isaiah 38:17) Looking back, he doesn't call it for nothing.
Right, baker. Hezekiah says, “Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish.” (Isaiah 38:17) He doesn't call it for nothing. He looks back and says it was for his welfare.
Yes, baker. Hezekiah says to the Lord, “You have cast all my sins behind Your back.” (Isaiah 38:17) All of them, not just the small ones. That's a thing worth smiling about.
That's the opposite direction, friend. Hezekiah says, “You have cast all my sins behind Your back.” (Isaiah 38:17) Behind, not before.

A book is a fair guess, but it isn't the picture Hezekiah paints. He says, “You have cast all my sins behind Your back.” (Isaiah 38:17) No book on the counter, just the Lord casting them behind His back.
That's it, baker. Hezekiah says, “The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today.” (Isaiah 38:19) He says "the living" twice, like he's still amazed he's one of them.

Priests are a reasonable guess, friend, but Hezekiah doesn't mention them here. He says, “The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today.” (Isaiah 38:19) He's talking about the living, and he's thanking the Lord himself.

I can see how you got there. But angels don't come up in this line. Hezekiah says, “The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today.” (Isaiah 38:19) His point is that the living can thank the Lord, and he's one of them.
Right, baker. Hezekiah says, “fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness.” (Isaiah 38:19) He's already thinking about the next generation. I'd pass that along too.
That's a reasonable word, but it isn't the one Hezekiah uses. He says, “fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness.” (Isaiah 38:19) Faithfulness is what he wants handed down.

Victories would make a good story, friend, but that's not the word in the verse. Hezekiah says, “fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness.” (Isaiah 38:19) The thing to pass on is the Lord's faithfulness.

Yes, baker. The text says, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.” (Isaiah 38:21) That's Isaiah's exact instruction. It's the one time I'll mention a food that isn't a cookie, because the Bible did first.
Olive oil sounds like a good guess, friend. But Isaiah says, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.” (Isaiah 38:21) The text names figs, so that's the one.

Balm is a fair thing to think of for a boil. But in this passage, Isaiah says, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.” (Isaiah 38:21) Figs are what he asks for.

That's right, baker. The text says, “And Hezekiah had asked, ‘What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?’” (Isaiah 38:22) I think a man who just got fifteen more years would want a sign about going back to the house of the LORD.

This one is True, friend. The text says, “And Hezekiah had asked, ‘What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?’” (Isaiah 38:22) He did ask, and it's right there in the last verse.
